name: Wrist and forearm
pattern: Small forearm moves: the wrist bends and straightens, the forearm turns, or the hand squeezes, while the elbow stays still.
setup: Sit with your forearms resting on your thighs or a bench, wrists just past the edge.
Hold a light bar or dumbbells, palms up for a wrist curl.
Elbows about 90°, forearms still on the support.

steps.text: Let the weight roll the hand back until the wrist is bent back as far as is comfortable.
Curl the wrist up as high as you can; only the hand moves.
Hold the top for a moment.
Lower slowly back to the stretch.

cues.cue: Forearms stay flat on the support; only the hands move.
cues.why: Keeping the elbow still isolates the wrist muscles instead of turning it into a curl.

cues.cue: Full, slow range, wrist bent back to curled up.
cues.why: Controlled lowering of the wrist extensors (the eccentric phase) helps tennis-elbow recovery.

cues.cue: For grip holds, keep the wrist slightly bent back, about 25-35°.
cues.why: Grip is strongest near 35° of wrist extension; a straight or bent-down wrist cuts grip to two thirds or less.

cues.cue: Use light weights and higher reps.
cues.why: The forearm muscles are small and the wrist lever is short; heavy loads strain the wrist and elbow tendons.

breathing: Breathe normally; out as you curl.

tempo.note: Curl in 1 second, lower in about 3.

mistakes.name: Forearms lift
mistakes.looks: The elbows and forearms come off the support to help move the weight.
mistakes.fix: Press your forearms down and use less weight.
mistakes.why: The arm muscles take over from the wrist muscles.

mistakes.name: Tiny range
mistakes.looks: The hand only flicks a few degrees up and down.
mistakes.fix: Lower to a full stretch each rep, then curl all the way up.
mistakes.why: Short, fast reps skip the slow lowering that loads the tendon in a useful way.

mistakes.name: Wrist bent down in grip holds
mistakes.looks: During a hold or squeeze the wrist bends down toward the palm.
mistakes.fix: Keep the knuckles slightly back, wrist bent back about 30°.
mistakes.why: Grip strength falls sharply when the wrist leaves its best position.

safety: Tennis elbow: start with slow lowering only, light load; mild pain that settles within a day is usually acceptable, sharp pain is not.
Wrist pain or recent wrist injury: reduce the range and load and get advice.

variants.change: Standing, bar held behind or in front of the thighs: same wrist motion, arms hang.
Thumbs up: the wrist moves side to side (radial deviation).
Finger curl: let the bar roll down to the fingertips, then close the hand.
Cable or band: tension stays on through the whole range.

subtypes.name: Reverse wrist curl
subtypes.change: Palms down (forearm 85); the back of the hand lifts up (wrist extension).

subtypes.name: Pronation and supination
subtypes.change: Forearm rests on a bench or the arm hangs, hand holds one end of a dumbbell or hammer; turn the palm down, then up.

subtypes.name: Grip and pinch hold
subtypes.change: Squeeze a gripper, pinch plates or hold a hang board; wrist slightly bent back.

subtypes.name: Wrist roller
subtypes.change: Arms straight forward at shoulder height; roll the rope up by turning the hands one after the other, then lower it slowly.

motion.basis: Best grip wrist angle (about 35° extension) from odriscoll1992; slow eccentric emphasis from tyler2010. Wrist ranges are typical active range (about 60° flexion, 50-60° extension) used by us as estimates; seated posture is convention. No kinematic study of these exercises was found.

sources.cite: O'Driscoll SW, Horii E, Ness R, Cahalan TD, Richards RR, An KN. The relationship between wrist position, grasp size, and grip strength. J Hand Surg Am. 1992;17(1):169-177.

Tyler TF, Thomas GC, Nicholas SJ, McHugh MP. Addition of isolated wrist extensor eccentric exercise to standard treatment for chronic lateral epicondylosis: a prospective randomized trial. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 2010;19(6):917-922.
